predecessors.name: Western Chalukya Empire
predecessors.text: the Hoysala home country, which the Hoysalas held as Chalukya feudatories before Vishnuvardhana 'asserted his independence'

successors.name: Vijayanagara Empire
successors.text: 'the sovereign territories of the Hoysala Kingdom were merged with the areas administered by Harihara I' in the Tungabhadra region (1343)

ledger.x: c. 1108: the Hoysalas rise under Vishnuvardhana. 'During the reign of King Vishnuvardhana (r. c. 1108-1152 CE), the Hoysalas fought decisive campaigns against the Cholas'; the dynasty 'gained prominence under King Vishnuvardhana' and he fought the Western Chalukyas 'asserting his independence from them'. The page…
1116: Vishnuvardhana takes back Gangavadi.

c. 1118: Vishnuvardhana fights the Chalukyas in the north. He 'fought Chalukyan armies at Kannegala (c.1118), took a fort at Hanagal, and defeated the Chalukyan commander Boppanna at Hallur (c.1120)'.

c. 1120: Banavasi and Humacha pass to the Hoysalas. After Hallur 'He then extended control over the Banavasi and Humacha regions'. The page puts both under c.1117-c.1120 without a year for the extension.

c. 1122: the northern advance stops at the Krishna. 'By c.1122, he had reached the Krishna river'; there the Sinda chief Achugi defeated him and he 'accepted Chalukya subordination for the time being'.

c. 1122: the Hoysalas accept Chalukya subordination. 'By c.1122, he had reached the Krishna river. Here he was defeated by the powerful Sinda chief Achugi, a commander loyal to the Chalukya emperor. Vishnuvardhana thus had to accept, for the time being, subordination to the Chalukya throne'; the Hoysala page…
1126 (bridge): the nominal tie lapses with Vikramaditya VI's death, as in western-chalukya-empire /ledger/26 (confidence 1 there too).
c. 1140: Vishnuvardhana pushes north of the Tungabhadra. 'He recaptured Hanagal, Uchchangi, and Bankapura and marched north of the Tungabhadra River up to Lakkundi' (c.1140).

c. 1178: Ballala II annexes Hangal. The page has 'the annexation of Hangal in c. 1178' and, in the same section, a Kalachuri commander seizing Hangal in c. 1179 after a failed attempt on Belvola-300; the two statements are not reconciled on the page. The previous holder is not named, so the counterpart is the place.
ledger.cp: Hangal (holder not named on the page)

ledger.x: c. 1179: the Kalachuris invade. 'a Kalachuri invasion into the Hoysala territory resulted in a truce'; 'By c. 1183, the Kalachuris themselves were in serious decline'.

c. 1179: the Kalachuris seize Hangal. 'But an attempt by him to invade Belvola-300 in c. 1179 led to his defeat by Kalachuri commander Sankama who seized Hangal'; the truce that follows had Ballala II 'agreeing to accept nominal subordination' (a nominal tie not drawn as a vassal event). The page does not say when…
c. 1179: the Kalachuri invasion ends in a truce.

c. 1190: Banavasi falls to Ballala II. 'Ballala II led several expeditions to Banavasi against the exiled Chalukya King Someshvara VI and defeated him by c. 1190' (Someshvara VI, as the page writes it; the first version said the numeral did not match and named western-chalukya-empire, which ends in 1187 in its own…
ledger.cp: Western Chalukya rump of Someshvara VI (Banavasi)

ledger.x: c. 1191: Ballala II meets the Yadavas. 'In c. 1191, the Hoysala monarch gained the upper hand over Yadava Bhillama V in the critical battles of Soratur and Lakkundi.'
c. 1191: the battles of Soratur and Lakkundi go to the Hoysalas.

c. 1192: Ballala II is emperor of Karnataka. 'In c. 1191, the Hoysala monarch gained the upper hand over Yadava Bhillama V in the critical battles of Soratur and Lakkundi'; 'By c. 1192, Ballala II had crowned himself the emperor over the entire modern Karnataka region' with 'the northern boundaries of the Hoysala…
c. 1212: the Yadavas take the north back. 'After c. 1212, he lost all these territories north of the Tungabhadra River to Yadava king Singhana II.'
1217: Ballala II defeats the Pandyas in the Chola country.
1217: the Pandyas are repulsed and the Chola king restored.
1220: Hoysala hegemony over the Chola kingdom.
1220: Hoysala hegemony over the Pandya kingdom (same sentence, 1220-1245).

c. 1225: a Hoysala foothold in the Tamil country. 'The Hoysalas extended their foothold in modern-day Tamil Nadu around 1225', 'making the city of Kannanur Kuppam near Srirangam a provincial capital'.
1236: Magadai Mandalam.
1245: the Hoysala hegemony over the Chola kingdom ends with the span the page gives ('From 1220 to 1245').
1245: the Hoysala hegemony over the Pandya kingdom ends (same sentence).

c. 1262 (bridge): the Pandya war reaches Kannanur. Vira Someshwara 'stayed back at Kannanur with Ramanatha where he was killed in a war with Sadayavarman Sundara Pandyan I'; the page gives no year for the war or for his death, and his reign ends in 1263, so 1262-1263 is a bridge (confidence 1).
1263 (bridge): Vira Someshwara is killed and the war ends in a Pandya success; the page gives no treaty.
1263 (bridge): the Tamil holdings are lost.

c. 1295 (bridge): Veera Ballala III recaptures the Tamil holdings. 'Toward the end of the 13th century, Veera Ballala III recaptured territory in the Tamil country which had been lost during a Pandya uprising'; the Veera Ballala III page adds that 'the northern and southern…

c. 1300: the court moves to Tiruvannamalai. Infobox 'Tiruvannamalai (1300-1343)'; the text has Veera Ballala III 'stationed himself at Tiruvannamalai' against the northern invaders and the Madurai Sultanate. The Veera Ballala III page has the realm run from Halebidu and the refuge at Tiruvannamalai only after the…
26 February 1311: Malik Kafur plunders Halebidu.
1311: Veera Ballala III submits.
1311: Veera Ballala III becomes tributary to Delhi.

c. 1318 (bridge): the tribute stops. After 'By 1318' the page says Ballala III 'refused to pay tribute and withdrew from his earlier pact to support the Delhi Sultanate as a vassal'; it gives no exact year and no trigger, so 1318 is a bridge (confidence 1).
c. 1327: the Tughluq army sacks Halebidu again. Halebidu was 'plundered for a second time' when Tughluq sent an army south; Veera Ballala III 'had to find refuge in Tiruvannamalai'.

c. 1327: the sack ends; the page gives no date and no treaty, only that Veera Ballala III kept resisting from Tiruvannamalai. By c. 1336 'all Hindu kingdoms of south India with the exception of the Hoysala Empire had been defeated'.
c. 1342: the war with the Madurai Sultanate. 'a decisive war that would end the Hoysala fortunes was fought at Kannanur' (c. 1342-3); the Madurai Sultanate was established c. 1335-6.
1343: Veera Ballala III is killed.
1343: the Hoysala kingdom ends.

wars.name: Hoysala-Chola war for Gangavadi
wars.outcome: Vishnuvardhana defeats the Chola general Adiyamma near Talakadu in 1116, recovers Gangavadi and chases the Cholas to Vellore.

wars.name: Vishnuvardhana's wars with the Western Chalukyas
wars.outcome: The Hoysalas take Banavasi and Humacha after Hallur (c.

wars.name: Yadava reconquest north of the Tungabhadra
wars.outcome: 'After c. 1212, he lost all these territories north of the Tungabhadra River to Yadava king Singhana II.'

wars.name: Hoysala intervention in the Chola-Pandya war
wars.outcome: Prince Narasimha II repulses the Pandyas and restores Kulothunga III; the Hoysalas gain a hegemony over the Chola and Pandya kingdoms (1220-1245).

wars.name: Hoysala-Pandya war under Vira Someshwara
wars.outcome: Vira Someshwara 'stayed back at Kannanur with Ramanatha where he was killed in a war with' Sadayavarman Sundara Pandyan I; the Tamil holdings are lost 'during a Pandya uprising' and recaptured by Veera Ballala III toward the end of the 13th century.

wars.name: Delhi Sultanate invasions of the Hoysalas
wars.outcome: Halebidu is sacked on 26 February 1311 and again c.

certainty.note: No page opened gives a boundary or a treaty line; the northern marches (Banavasi, Hangal, Lakkundi, the Krishna) changed hands with every war, and the Tamil holdings are circles round Kannanur.
